subject: Climate & Environment
title: Agricultural Runoff
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Agricultural Runoff.

hook.text: Rain washes fertilizer off farm fields and into rivers. What feeds crops can kill lakes.

buildup.text: Excess nitrogen and phosphorus flow downstream, feeding algae in rivers, lakes, and coasts.

discovery.text: Algae blooms consume all the oxygen, creating dead zones where fish cannot survive.

twist.text: The Gulf of Mexico dead zone covers 6,000 square miles every summer — the size of Connecticut.

climax.text: Reducing runoff means changing how millions of farms apply fertilizer — a massive challenge.

punchline.text: What makes the land green can turn the water lifeless.

quiz.question: What causes dead zones in coastal waters?
options: Algae fed by farm fertilizer runoff
Volcanic activity on the sea floor

details.summary: Agricultural runoff carries fertilizers, pesticides, and animal waste into rivers, lakes, and coastal waters. Excess nitrogen and phosphorus trigger algal blooms that consume oxygen and create dead zones, killing fish and degrading water quality for drinking and recreation downstream.
details.whyItMatters: Runoff is the largest source of water pollution globally. Algal blooms and dead zones destroy aquatic ecosystems and contaminate drinking water supplies for millions of people.
takeaways: Fertilizer runoff causes toxic algal blooms in waterways
Dead zones kill fish by depleting dissolved oxygen
Agriculture is the top source of water pollution globally

faq.question: What is the largest dead zone in the world?
faq.answer: The Gulf of Mexico dead zone, fed by Mississippi River nutrient runoff from Midwest agriculture, reaches up to 22,000 square kilometers in summer. Oxygen levels drop so low that fish and shrimp flee or die, devastating Gulf fisheries.

faq.question: How can farmers reduce runoff pollution?
faq.answer: Practices include precision fertilizer application, cover crops that absorb excess nutrients, buffer strips of vegetation along waterways, no-till farming that reduces soil erosion, and constructed wetlands that filter runoff before it reaches rivers.
